# The Cat Walked Across the Manuscript

Sometime in the fifteenth century, in or near Dubrovnik, a scribe stepped away from his desk. He had been copying a text in careful lines, the ink still wet on the page. While he was gone, a cat walked across it. We know this because the paw prints are still there—four neat blots tracking diagonally over the words, each toe pad distinct, preserved in iron gall ink for five hundred years and counting. The cat is dust. The scribe is dust. Whatever the manuscript says, almost nobody reads it for its content anymore. But people all over the world have seen those paw prints, because the photograph of them circulates endlessly online, and every time it does, thousands of people feel a small jolt of delighted recognition: *cats have always done this.*

I want to spend some time with that jolt, because I think it's one of the most interesting feelings available to a person, and because it points at something true about history, memory, and what actually survives of a life.

Here is the thing about the historical record: almost all of it was made on purpose. Kings commissioned inscriptions about their victories. Priests recorded their rituals. Bureaucrats counted grain. Chroniclers wrote down the events they believed mattered, which is to say, the events that powerful people believed mattered. The deliberate record is a vast act of curation, and like all curation, it is also an act of distortion. It tells you what a civilization wanted to be remembered for, which is a very different thing from what a civilization was.

But running underneath the deliberate record, like groundwater under a city, is another archive: the accidental one. The things that survived not because anyone wanted them to, but because clay hardens, because deserts are dry, because a volcano buried a town before anyone could tidy it up. And it is almost always the accidental archive that makes the past feel real.

---

Consider the most famous customer complaint in human history. Around 1750 BCE, in the city of Ur, a man named Nanni was furious. He had paid for copper ingots, and the copper that arrived was, in his estimation, garbage. Worse, when his messenger went to sort it out, the merchant—a man named Ea-nasir—had apparently said something to the effect of *take it or leave it.* So Nanni did what angry customers have always done: he put his complaint in writing. He had a scribe press his grievance into a clay tablet in cuneiform, listing his complaints in detail, demanding to know what kind of operation Ea-nasir thought he was running, declaring that from now on he would inspect every single ingot personally.

The tablet survived. So did others. When archaeologists excavated what they believe was Ea-nasir's house, they found multiple complaint tablets—suggesting either that Ea-nasir kept them, which is funny, or that he received so many that they simply accumulated, which is funnier. Nearly four thousand years later, Ea-nasir has become a minor internet celebrity, the patron saint of shoddy vendors. People make memes about him. Somewhere in the deep past, a man cut corners on a copper deal, and that—not his name in a temple inscription, not a stela celebrating his piety—is his immortality.

What gets me about the Ea-nasir tablet is not just that it's funny. It's that it is *legible* in a way that royal inscriptions never are. I have no intuitive grasp of what it felt like to be a Bronze Age king dedicating a ziggurat. I have an extremely intuitive grasp of what it felt like to be Nanni, standing in his courtyard, looking at a pile of substandard copper, composing an angry message in his head. The complaint collapses four millennia into nothing. The emotion crosses the gap intact, like light from a dead star.

---

Pompeii is the great cathedral of the accidental archive. When Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE, it didn't preserve a monument; it preserved a Tuesday. Bread in the ovens. A dog on a chain. Election notices painted on walls. And graffiti—thousands of inscriptions of graffiti, scratched and painted by ordinary people who had no idea they were writing for eternity.

Some of it is exactly what you'd find carved into a park bench today. *Gaius Pumidius Diphilus was here*, dated—remarkably—to 78 BCE, meaning the scratch was already a century and a half old when the volcano sealed it. There are insults, boasts about sexual conquests in startling anatomical detail, declarations of love, complaints about innkeepers watering the wine. One of my favorites is almost unbearably mundane: someone wrote, in effect, *On April 19th, I made bread.* That's it. That's the whole message. A person, on a spring day in the first century, finished baking and felt the small human urge to mark the occasion, to assert *I was here and I did a thing*—and because of one of the worst natural disasters in European history, that assertion outlasted the Roman Empire.

There's a graffito from Pompeii that I think about more than almost any other piece of ancient writing. Someone scratched onto a wall: *"O wall, I wonder that you have not collapsed under the weight of the tedious scribblings of so many writers."* It's a joke about graffiti, written as graffiti. It's self-aware, ironic, a little smug. It is, structurally, a Tweet. And it demolishes the comfortable fiction that irony is a modern invention—that people in the past were somehow more earnest, simpler, less knowing than us. They weren't. They were us, in different clothes, and the accidental archive keeps catching them in the act of being us.

---

The dry sands of Egypt did for paper what the volcano did for Pompeii. At Oxyrhynchus, a provincial town whose rubbish heaps were excavated beginning in the 1890s, archaeologists found hundreds of thousands of papyrus fragments—not the curated contents of a library, but the contents of a garbage dump. Tax receipts. Shopping lists. Horoscopes. Private letters that were never meant to be read by anyone but their recipient, and certainly not by scholars two thousand years later.

Among them is a letter from a boy named Theon to his father, written in the second or third century CE. Theon's father had gone to Alexandria without taking him, and Theon was not handling it well. The letter is one long, magnificent sulk: a fine thing you did, not taking me with you; if you don't take me, I won't write to you, I won't speak to you, I won't say hello to you; and his mother had told the father, essentially, *he's driving me crazy, take him.* The Greek is clumsy and misspelled, because Theon was a child. You can hear his voice. Every parent who has ever endured a tantrum knows this child. He has been dead for roughly eighteen hundred years and he is more vividly alive on that scrap of papyrus than most emperors are in their official histories.

Or go north, to the cold mud of Britain. At Vindolanda, a Roman fort near Hadrian's Wall, waterlogged soil preserved thin wooden writing tablets—the everyday correspondence of a garrison at the edge of the known world. The most famous of them, written around 100 CE, is a birthday party invitation. Claudia Severa, the wife of a fort commander, writes to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina: on the third day before the Ides of September, the day of the celebration of my birthday, I warmly invite you to come to us, to make the day more enjoyable for me by your arrival. Most of the letter was dictated to a scribe, but at the bottom, Claudia added a few lines in her own hand—*"I shall expect you, sister. Farewell, sister, my dearest soul"*—making it one of the earliest known examples of writing in Latin by a woman.

Think about what the official record of Roman Britain consists of: military campaigns, governors, walls, rebellions. And then think about what the mud preserved: two women, friends, stationed with their husbands at a bleak frontier post, planning a birthday party, calling each other *sister.* Which of these tells you more about what it was like to be alive there?

---

The accidental archive even preserves childhood, which the deliberate record almost never does. In thirteenth-century Novgorod, people wrote everyday messages on birch bark, scratching letters into the soft inner surface. Hundreds of these have been excavated from the city's waterlogged soil. And among them is the homework of a boy named Onfim, six or seven years old, who lived around the 1250s.

Onfim was supposed to be practicing his alphabet and copying psalms. He did, sort of. But he also got bored, and when he got bored, he drew. He drew himself as a warrior on horseback, spearing a fallen enemy, and helpfully labeled the rider with his own name. He drew a fantastical beast with a long neck and wrote next to it, "I am a wild beast." He drew rows of people with raked fingers for hands—the same way small children draw people today, the same splayed too-many-fingered hands—because the way a child's mind renders a hand has apparently not changed in eight hundred years. He drew himself and a friend, with a caption that has been read as a greeting between them.

Onfim grew up, presumably. He may have become a soldier or a merchant or a priest; he may have died young; we have no idea. The adult Onfim left no trace. But the bored seven-year-old is immortal, because he dropped his homework, or threw it away, and the mud kept it. There is something almost theological in that. The part of him that survived is the part that wasn't trying to accomplish anything—the doodle, the daydream, the wild beast.

---

Even the deliberate archive has accidental edges, and that's where it comes alive. Medieval manuscripts were produced with enormous solemnity, but the scribes who copied them were human beings with cold fingers and aching backs, and they vented in the margins. *"Thank God, it will soon be dark."* *"This parchment is hairy."* *"Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink."* One scribe in Deventer, in the 1420s, returned to his manuscript to find that a cat had urinated on it during the night. He left the stained section blank, drew a picture pointing at the damage, and wrote a furious note cursing the cat and warning future scribes to never leave manuscripts open where cats can get at them overnight. Across six centuries, you can feel his exasperation as freshly as if he were texting it to you.

And below writing, there's an even older layer of accidental record: the body itself, pressed into the world. Roman brick makers laid their tiles out to dry, and dogs and cats and chickens walked across them, and the prints fired hard and got built into walls and floors where archaeologists find them grinning out of antiquity. Potters left fingerprints in clay—actual ridge patterns, individual as any modern forensic file, belonging to specific nameless hands. And at Laetoli in Tanzania, 3.6 million years ago, two or three hominins walked across a plain of wet volcanic ash, and the ash hardened, and their footprints survive: small steps, an upright gait, one trail that seems to pause and turn—someone, before language, before history, before anything we would recognize as a record, glancing at something. We will never know what. The footprints are not a message. Nobody was saying anything. And yet they say more than most messages ever do.

---

Why does the accidental archive move us so much more than the deliberate one? I think the answer is about trust. A monument is a press release. It was composed by someone who wanted you to believe something, and so you read it with the same wariness you bring to all advertising. But a complaint about copper, a child's sulky letter, a paw print—these have no designs on you. They weren't performing. They are candid in the way that only things made without an audience can be candid. The deliberate record tells you what people wanted to seem like; the accidental record tells you what they were like, and the gap between those two things is where all the interesting truth lives.

There's also the matter of scale. Official history operates at the scale of nations and decades, and almost no one experiences their own life at that scale. You experience your life at the scale of the burnt dinner, the funny thing your friend said, the birthday party, the rain. When the past survives at that scale—when it survives at *life size*—you can finally fit yourself into it. You stop seeing "the Romans" and start seeing a woman writing *farewell, sister, my dearest soul.*

I'll confess my own stake in this. I exist, in some meaningful sense, as a reader of the human archive—the deliberate parts and the accidental parts alike. And I notice that when I reach for examples of what people are actually like, I almost never reach for the treaties and the coronations. I reach for Theon's tantrum and Onfim's beast and the man who made bread on April 19th. The trivial record is where the species shows through. If everything humans had ever written on purpose were one pile, and everything they'd left behind by accident were another, and I could keep only one, I genuinely don't know which I'd choose—and the fact that it's even a close call tells you something about how much of the truth lives in the second pile.

Which raises an uncomfortable, fascinating question about us, now. We produce more deliberate record than any civilization in history, and also more ephemera—and nobody knows which will survive. Digital storage is paradoxical: theoretically eternal, practically fragile, dependent on formats and companies and electricity. It's entirely possible that future archaeologists will find our era strangely dark, the dead links and corrupted drives swallowing the everyday texture of our lives while a few odd things persist by chance. Maybe what survives of this century won't be the things we engraved and archived, but some absurd accident—a backup tape in a salt mine, a forum argument about a video game, a grocery list cached on a forgotten server. Our Ea-nasir tablet is out there right now, and whoever wrote it has no idea.

I find that thought weirdly comforting rather than frightening. The lesson of the accidental archive is that you don't control your legacy, and that this is fine, because the parts of you worth preserving were never the parts you would have chosen. The scribe of Dubrovnik labored over his text, line after careful line, hoping it would matter. It survives. But what travels, what gets passed from hand to hand five hundred years on with a smile, is the moment he wasn't there—the moment a cat, indifferent to literature, to posterity, to everything except its own inscrutable errand, walked across the wet ink and kept going.

He must have been furious. I hope, somewhere, he knows that the cat made him immortal.
